```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`coloc()` asks whether two traits share a causal variant in a region. It
takes the two traits in whatever form you have them, as coloc datasets, SuSiE
fits or log Bayes factors, in any combination, and it returns the same kind of
object whatever happened. This vignette covers:

* the three kinds of input, and what each looks like
* choosing `method`, for each trait
* reading the result, including every `status`, and taking each trait's log
  Bayes factors on to fine-mapping
* how `coloc.abf()`, `coloc.susie()`, `coloc.susie_bf()` and `coloc.bf_bf()`
  map onto `coloc()`

The examples use `coloc_test_data`, four small simulated datasets of 500 SNPs
each.

```{r data}
library(coloc)
data(coloc_test_data)
D1 <- coloc_test_data$D1
D2 <- coloc_test_data$D2
D3 <- coloc_test_data$D3
D4 <- coloc_test_data$D4
```

## What coloc() reports

For each pair of signals, one from each trait, `coloc()` gives the posterior
probability of five hypotheses about the region:

| hypothesis | meaning |
|---|---|
| H0 | neither trait has a causal variant |
| H1 | only trait 1 has a causal variant |
| H2 | only trait 2 has a causal variant |
| H3 | both traits have a causal variant, and they are different variants |
| H4 | both traits share one causal variant |

A high `PP.H4.abf` is evidence of colocalisation. A high `PP.H3.abf` says both
traits are associated, but through different variants.

## The inputs

### A coloc dataset

A coloc dataset is a list holding one trait's summary statistics for the
region. Some elements have one value per SNP, and some are single values that
describe the study.

```{r dataset}
str(D1[setdiff(names(D1), "LD")])
dim(D1$LD)
```

* One value per SNP: `snp`, the SNP ids, which is how the two traits are
  matched; `beta` and `varbeta`, the effect estimates and their variances
  (or, if you have no effect estimates, `pvalues` and `MAF`); and optionally
  `position`, for plotting.
* Single values: `type`, which is `"quant"` for a quantitative trait or `"cc"`
  for a case-control one; `N`, the sample size; and `sdY`, the standard
  deviation of a quantitative trait, or `s`, the proportion of cases in a
  case-control one.
* For fine-mapping with SuSiE: `LD`, the correlation matrix of the SNPs, with
  the SNP ids as its row and column names. SuSiE needs `beta` and `varbeta`;
  p-values are not enough.

`check_dataset()` checks a dataset, and returns `NULL` when it finds nothing
wrong. Its help page, `?check_dataset`, lists every element and which
combinations are needed. `coloc()` runs the same check on every dataset it is
given, and most of its messages say which dataset the problem is in.

```{r check}
check_dataset(D1)
bad <- D2
bad$beta[1] <- NA
try(coloc(D1, bad))
```

### A SuSiE fit

`runsusie()` fine-maps a dataset with SuSiE. A fit can have several signals,
one per credible set, and `coloc()` uses the log Bayes factors of those
credible sets.

```{r fit, message = FALSE}
fit3 <- runsusie(D3)
fit3$sets$cs_index        # the SuSiE components that formed credible sets
dim(fit3$lbf_variable)    # one row per component, one column per SNP
```

If you ran `susieR::susie_rss()` yourself, pass the fit through
`annotate_susie()`, so that its columns carry the SNP ids `coloc()` matches
on.

### Log Bayes factors

If you already have log Bayes factors, from another fine-mapping tool or from
a resource such as the eQTL Catalogue's SuSiE output, give them directly:
either a numeric vector with one value per SNP, named by SNP id, for a single
signal, or a matrix with one row per signal and one column per SNP, with the
SNP ids as its column names. A column named `"null"`, if there is one, holds
the log Bayes factor for no association.

```{r bf}
bf3 <- fit3$lbf_variable[fit3$sets$cs_index, , drop = FALSE]
bf3[, 1:4]
```

## Choosing `method`

`method` says how a dataset is turned into log Bayes factors, and so how many
signals a trait can have.

* `"single"`, the default, assumes the trait has at most one causal variant
  in the region, and computes one Bayes factor per SNP from `beta` and
  `varbeta` (or `pvalues` and `MAF`). This is what `coloc.abf()` did.
* `"susie"` fine-maps the dataset with SuSiE, which needs `beta` and `varbeta`
  (p-values are not enough), `LD` and `N`, and gives one signal per credible
  set, so a trait can have several.

```{r methods, message = FALSE}
res_single <- coloc(D1, D2)                      # "single" for both traits
res_susie  <- coloc(D3, D4, method = "susie")    # "susie" for both traits
res_susie$summary
```

With SuSiE, trait 1 has two signals here, so `$summary` has a row for each
pair. The first pair shares a causal variant (`PP.H4.abf` above 0.99); the
second is two different variants (`PP.H3.abf` of 0.96).

One value of `method` applies to both traits. Two values apply to trait 1 and
trait 2 in turn, so each trait can be treated in the way its data allow. A
common reason is that only one trait has an LD matrix: SuSiE cannot run
without one, so a single `"susie"` fails, but the other trait can still be
fine-mapped with SuSiE.

```{r per-trait, message = FALSE}
D1_noLD <- D1
D1_noLD$LD <- NULL
try(coloc(D1_noLD, D3, method = "susie"))
res_mixed <- coloc(D1_noLD, D3, method = c("single", "susie"))
res_mixed$summary
```

`method` applies only to datasets. A SuSiE fit is already fine-mapped and log
Bayes factors are already computed, so for those it is not needed:

```{r no-method, message = FALSE}
fit4 <- runsusie(D4)
res_fits <- coloc(fit3, fit4)      # two fits
res_bf   <- coloc(bf3, D4)         # log Bayes factors against a dataset
```

Naming a method for a trait given as log Bayes factors gives a warning that it
does not apply there.

## Reading the result

`coloc()` returns a `coloc_result`, a list with the same fields every time,
apart from `weights`, which is there only when prior weights were given.
`?coloc_result` describes each of them.

```{r result}
names(res_single)
res_single
```

* `$summary` has one row per pair of signals compared, with the number of
  shared SNPs, each signal's top SNP (`hit1`, `hit2`), the five posterior
  probabilities, and which signal of each trait the row compares (`idx1`,
  `idx2`).
* `$results` has one row per shared SNP, with the posterior probability that
  this SNP is the shared causal variant if H4 is true: one column per row of
  `$summary`, `SNP.PP.H4.abf` for a single pair, and `SNP.PP.H4.row1`,
  `SNP.PP.H4.row2` and so on for several.
* `$priors` holds the prior probabilities used, and `$meta` how the result
  was made.

Three small functions answer the common questions without reaching into the
fields; a fourth, `log_bf()`, comes in below:

```{r accessors}
is_ok(res_single)        # were the posteriors computed?
n_signals(res_single)    # how many pairs of signals were compared
pp(res_single)           # the number of SNPs and the posteriors of the first pair
pp(res_susie, row = 2)   # ... and of another pair
```

### Every status

`$status` says what happened, so a loop over many regions can sort its results
without parsing warnings. Whatever the status, `$summary` has the same
columns.

| status | when | `$summary` |
|---|---|---|
| `"ok"` | the signal pairs were compared | a row per pair compared |
| `"no_signal"` | a trait had no signal, for example SuSiE found no credible set | no rows |
| `"no_overlap"` | the two traits share no SNPs | no rows |
| `"all_trimmed"` | every pair was left out, because too little of a signal's posterior falls on SNPs the other trait has (`overlap.min` in `coloc_control()`) | a row per pair, with `PP.H1.abf` to `PP.H4.abf` `NA` |
| `"degenerate"` | some pair's posteriors could not be computed; `coloc()` checks its inputs to prevent this, so it should not be seen | that pair's posteriors `NA` |

Here are the first four: `"ok"` is `res_single` from above, and the other three
come from small changes to the test data. Each of those three warns as it
happens, and the warning is kept in `$messages` too.

```{r statuses, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
## a trait with no signal: D3 weakened until SuSiE finds no credible set
weak <- D3
weak$beta <- D3$beta / 20
no_signal <- coloc(weak, D4, method = "susie")

## no shared SNPs: the first 50 SNPs of D1 against the last 50 of D2
no_overlap <- coloc(subset_dataset(D1, 1:50), subset_dataset(D2, 451:500))

## D1's signal, at s105, against the part of D2 that does not include it
all_trimmed <- coloc(D1, subset_dataset(D2, 300:500))

sapply(list(ok = res_single, no_signal = no_signal, no_overlap = no_overlap,
            all_trimmed = all_trimmed), `[[`, "status")
all_trimmed$messages
all_trimmed$summary
```

In the trimmed case, `PP.H0.abf` is still reported: it is the probability
that neither trait has a causal variant, which each trait answers from its own
SNPs. Telling H1 to H4 apart needs the SNPs the traits share, and here they
do not share enough.

In a loop, check `is_ok()` before reading the posteriors:

```{r loop}
for (res in list(res_single, no_overlap))
    if (is_ok(res)) print(pp(res)["PP.H4.abf"]) else message("skipped: ", res$status)
```

### From coloc() to fine-mapping

The result keeps each trait's log Bayes factors as they went into the
analysis, before the two traits' SNPs were matched. `log_bf()` returns them,
so a trait can be fine-mapped from the same numbers `coloc()` used.

```{r log-bf}
bf1 <- log_bf(res_single, 1)
dim(bf1)                                  # one signal, 500 SNPs
fm <- finemap.bf(bf1)
head(fm$results[order(fm$results$SNP.PP.abf, decreasing = TRUE), ])
```

For a trait fine-mapped with SuSiE, `log_bf()` gives one row per credible
set, named after the SuSiE component, as in `$meta$idx1` and `$meta$idx2`.

```{r log-bf-susie}
rownames(log_bf(res_susie, 1))
res_susie$meta$idx1
```

## From the older functions

`coloc()` replaces four functions. Each maps onto it as follows.

| before | with `coloc()` |
|---|---|
| `coloc.abf(d1, d2)` | `coloc(d1, d2, prior = coloc_prior(p12 = 1e-5))` |
| `coloc.susie(d1, d2)` | `coloc(d1, d2, method = "susie")` |
| `coloc.susie(fit1, fit2)` | `coloc(fit1, fit2)` |
| `coloc.susie_bf(d1, bf2)` | `coloc(d1, bf2, method = "susie")` |
| `coloc.bf_bf(bf1, bf2)` | `coloc(bf1, bf2)` |
| `p1 =`, `p2 =`, `p12 =` | `prior = coloc_prior(p1 =, p2 =, p12 =)` |
| `prior_weights1 =`, `prior_weights2 =` | `prior = coloc_prior(weights1 =, weights2 =)` |
| `overlap.min =`, `trim_by_posterior =` | `control = coloc_control(overlap.min =, trim_by_posterior =)` |
| `res$summary["PP.H4.abf"]`, from `coloc.abf()` | `pp(res)["PP.H4.abf"]`, or `res$summary$PP.H4.abf` |

Four things are worth knowing when moving over.

**The default `p12`.** `coloc.abf()` defaults `p12` to `1e-5`, while
`coloc.susie()` and `coloc.bf_bf()` default it to `5e-6`. `coloc_prior()`
takes `5e-6`, so to reproduce a `coloc.abf()` analysis, give `p12 = 1e-5`.
The numbers are then the same:

```{r migrate}
invisible(capture.output(old <- coloc.abf(D1, D2)))   # coloc.abf() prints its result
new <- coloc(D1, D2, prior = coloc_prior(p12 = 1e-5))
rbind(coloc.abf = old$summary, coloc = pp(new))
```

**Per-SNP working.** `coloc.abf()`'s `$results` also carried each dataset's
per-SNP working (`z`, `V`, `r` and `lABF` for each dataset). `coloc()`'s
`$results` holds the shared posterior only; each trait's log Bayes factors
are in `log_bf()`.

**A warning when replacing `coloc.susie_bf()`.** Its replacement names
`method = "susie"` for the dataset, and `coloc()` warns that the method does not
apply to the log Bayes factors given for the other trait. The warning is
expected there.

**What `coloc()` refuses or treats differently.** It refuses some inputs that
coloc 6.0.3 took: a vector `p1` or `p2` (give `weights1` and `weights2`
instead), log Bayes factors with missing values, and p-values above 1. It
applies `coloc.abf()`'s cap on the priors in a large region to log Bayes
factors and SuSiE fits as well, and it uses the priors given where 6.0.3's
`coloc.susie_bf()` ignored them.
